title: "Patching & Windowing"
subtitle: "Turn a time series into windows you can measure"
---

```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys, pathlib
sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path.cwd() / "src"))
from lectures import plotting, datasets
from lectures.plotting import INK, COOL, WARM, CRASH, BAND, GRID, PANEL, despine
plotting.set_style("notes")
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch
import einx                      # linear algebra with the axes spelled out
from jaxtyping import Float      # shape annotations: Float[Array, "n_days"]

Array = np.ndarray
R = datasets.load_returns()
```

So far each measure took two *scalar* columns — one number per day.  But a real
signal often lives across a **window of days**, not a single one, and a real book
is many columns at once.  **Patching** is the move that turns a scalar series into
vectors and blocks: cut the series into overlapping windows and treat each window
as one sample.

This is a hands-on tutorial — *how* to patch, *how* to look at patches, and *what*
becomes measurable once you have them.  The formal measures (total correlation,
mutual information) live in the [dependence](../dependence/index.qmd) chapter; here
we build the raw material they run on.

---

## 1 · What Is a Patch?

A **`w`-day patch** is a slice of `w` consecutive days.  Slide that window one day
at a time down a series and you get a *matrix*: each row is a window, each column a
position **within** the window.  One sample is now a `w`-vector.

```{python}
def windows(series: Float[Array, "n_days"], w: int) -> Float[Array, "n_windows w"]:
    """Sliding w-day patches of a 1-D series → (n − w + 1, w) matrix.

    patch:  Pᵢ = (sᵢ, sᵢ₊₁, …, sᵢ₊w₋₁)   — row i is the window starting on day i.
    """
    s: Float[Array, "n_days"] = np.asarray(series, dtype=float)
    if w <= 1:
        return s.reshape(-1, 1)
    # sliding_window_view is a no-copy view of shape (n − w + 1, w)
    return np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(s, w)

jpm: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R["JPM"].to_numpy()
P: Float[Array, "n_windows w"] = windows(jpm, 3)
print(f"JPM returns: {jpm.shape[0]} days")
print(f"windows(JPM, w=3): shape {P.shape}   (each row is a 3-day vector)")
print("first three patches:")
print(np.round(P[:3], 4))
```

`numpy`'s `sliding_window_view` builds the patch matrix as a *view* — no data is
copied, so even large series patch instantly.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Consecutive Windows Share Days
Patch 0 is days `(0,1,2)`, patch 1 is days `(1,2,3)` — they overlap in two days.
That overlap is not a bug: it is exactly the *redundancy across time* a window is
meant to expose.  We return to it in §4 and §6.
:::

### 1.1 · Two Ways to Place the Window: Causal vs Symmetric

A window of a *single* series turns the question "how does today relate to its own
recent past?" into a measurable block.  But *which* days you put in the window is a
modelling choice with a direction.  A **causal** (past-only) window ends on day `t`
and looks backward — `[s_{t-2}, s_{t-1}, s_t]` — so every feature is known *before*
the present.  A **symmetric** window centres on day `t` and peeks both ways —
`[s_{t-1}, s_t, s_{t+1}]` — which uses the future and is therefore off-limits for
forecasting, but fine for *describing* structure after the fact.

Both fall straight out of the same `windows()` helper: a `w=3` patch matrix already
*is* the causal block (row `i` ends on day `i+2`); shifting the index two days to the
left re-centres the very same rows into the symmetric block.

```{python}
s: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R["JPM"].to_numpy()    # one stationary-ish series: JPM returns
W: Float[Array, "n_windows w"] = windows(s, 3)     # every 3-day patch, row i = days (i, i+1, i+2)

# Causal:    a row ending on day t  -> [s_{t-2}, s_{t-1}, s_t]
# Symmetric: a row centred on day t -> [s_{t-1}, s_t, s_{t+1}]
# These are the SAME rows of W, just labelled by a different anchor day t.
causal:    Float[Array, "n_windows w"] = W         # row i is causal for t = i + 2
symmetric: Float[Array, "n_windows w"] = W         # row i is symmetric for t = i + 1

print("causal block  [s_{t-2}, s_{t-1}, s_t]   (past-only, ends on t):")
print(np.round(causal[:4], 4))
print("\nsymmetric block [s_{t-1}, s_t, s_{t+1}]  (centred, peeks ahead):")
print(np.round(symmetric[:4], 4))
print(f"\nboth blocks: shape {W.shape}   columns = window positions, rows = anchor days")
```

The two blocks hold identical numbers; only the *anchor day* `t` each row stands for
moves.  That is the whole point — and the raw material the labs reuse to ask whether
a measure of within-window structure even *notices* the difference.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Why Both, Side by Side
A causal window is what a forecaster is *allowed* to see; a symmetric window is what
a describer *would* see with hindsight.  Some statistics on these blocks care which
one you used (a forecast's error, a directional/Granger test); others — like
**total correlation**, which is a function of the *set* of positions and blind to
their order — do not.  This chapter only *builds* the two blocks; the labs run the
order-invariant measure on them.
:::

## 2 · Seeing the Window Slide

The clearest way to understand patching is to watch the window move.  Here is a
slice of the JPM series with three consecutive `w=10` windows drawn on top — each
shifted one day from the last.

```{python}
#| label: fig-patch-slide
#| fig-cap: "Three consecutive 10-day windows on the JPM return series, each one day to the right of the last. Patching slides this box down the whole series, stacking every position into a row of the patch matrix."
seg: Float[Array, "n_seg"] = jpm[60:120]
t = np.arange(seg.size)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.0))
ax.plot(t, seg, color=COOL, lw=1.4, marker="o", ms=3)
ax.axhline(0, color=INK, lw=0.6)
w = 10
for k, (start, col) in enumerate([(8, COOL), (9, WARM), (10, CRASH)]):
    y0, y1 = ax.get_ylim()
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((start - 0.4, y0 + 0.002 * k), w - 0.2,
                                (y1 - y0) - 0.004 * k, boxstyle="round,pad=0",
                                fill=False, edgecolor=col, lw=2, alpha=0.8))
    ax.text(start + w / 2 - 0.5, y1 - 0.004 - 0.004 * k, f"patch {k}",
            color=col, fontsize=9, ha="center", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xlabel("day (within a 60-day slice)"); ax.set_ylabel("JPM return")
ax.set_title("The window slides one day at a time", fontsize=12)
despine(ax); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## 3 · The Patch Matrix as a Picture

Stack every window into a matrix and you can *look at it* as an image: rows are
windows (time, top to bottom), columns are positions inside the window.  Do it on
**\|returns\|** (a proxy for volatility) and two things show up at once: **diagonal
streaks**, because one big day slides through the window positions as the window
moves (the visible signature of overlap), and **bright clusters**, stretches where
many large days bunch together — volatility clusters.

```{python}
#| label: fig-patch-matrix
#| fig-cap: "The |returns| patch matrix for JPM (w=21), 250 windows spanning the 2008–09 financial crisis. Each row is a 21-day window. A single turbulent day appears in 21 successive windows at a sliding position, so it draws a diagonal streak — the signature of the overlap between neighbouring windows. Where streaks bunch into bright regions, volatility is clustering (here, the crisis itself); dark stretches are calm."
A: Float[Array, "n_days"] = np.abs(jpm)
start = R.index.searchsorted("2008-09-01")     # anchor on the 2008 crisis
M: Float[Array, "n_windows w"] = windows(A, 21)[start:start + 250]   # 250 patches × 21 positions
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.6))
im = ax.imshow(M, aspect="auto", cmap="magma", interpolation="nearest")
ax.set_xlabel("position within window  (day 0 … 20)")
ax.set_ylabel("window index  (slides down the series →)")
ax.set_title("Each row is a 21-day patch of |returns|", fontsize=12)
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.04, pad=0.02, label="|return|")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## 4 · Overlapping vs Non-Overlapping

Two ways to cut patches.  **Sliding** windows move one day at a time (stride 1) and
overlap heavily — many windows, but neighbours share days.  **Non-overlapping**
windows tile the series (stride `w`) and reuse no day — fewer windows, cleaner but
coarser.  The choice is a modelling decision with a cost.

```{python}
#| label: fig-overlap
#| fig-cap: "Sliding (stride 1, overlapping) vs non-overlapping (stride w) windows over the same 24 days. Sliding gives many overlapping samples; tiling gives a handful of independent ones. Overlap can inflate apparent redundancy, so a finding should be checked against non-overlapping windows."
days = np.arange(24)
fig, (axT, axB) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9.5, 3.8), sharex=True)
for ax, stride, title, col in [
    (axT, 1, "sliding · stride 1 (overlapping)", COOL),
    (axB, 4, "non-overlapping · stride 4 (tiling)", CRASH),
]:
    ax.plot(days, np.zeros_like(days), "o", color=GRID, ms=4)
    starts = range(0, 24 - 4 + 1, stride)
    for i, s in enumerate(list(starts)[:8]):
        y = 0.12 + 0.10 * (i % 4 if stride == 1 else 0)
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((s - 0.3, y), 4 - 0.4, 0.08,
                                    boxstyle="round,pad=0.02", facecolor=col,
                                    edgecolor=col, alpha=0.5))
    ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_ylim(-0.1, 0.6)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11, loc="left", color=col, fontweight="bold")
    despine(ax)
axB.set_xlabel("day"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## 5 · Patching More Than One Variable

The payoff is comparing **blocks**.  Patch two series on the *same* days and you get
two aligned matrices — a window of X against the contemporaneous window of Y.

```{python}
#| label: fig-two-blocks
#| fig-cap: "JPM and BAC patched on the same days (w=10), 120 windows from the 2008 crisis as aligned images (red = up day, blue = down). Both share the diagonal-streak texture of overlap; the point here is the *alignment* — row i is the same 10 calendar days for each bank. The two panels light up in step — a between-block measure compares these aligned rows and finds the banks move together (cross-correlation ≈ 0.83 at matching positions)."
w = 10
b_start = R.index.searchsorted("2008-09-01")    # the same crisis window
# two aligned blocks: row i is the SAME 10 calendar days for each bank
Pj: Float[Array, "n_windows w"] = windows(jpm, w)[b_start:b_start + 120]
Pb: Float[Array, "n_windows w"] = windows(R["BAC"].to_numpy(), w)[b_start:b_start + 120]
vmax = np.abs(np.concatenate([Pj, Pb])).max()
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.6), sharey=True)
for ax, Pm, name, cmap in [(axL, Pj, "JPM", "RdBu_r"), (axR, Pb, "BAC", "RdBu_r")]:
    ax.imshow(Pm, aspect="auto", cmap=cmap, vmin=-vmax, vmax=vmax)
    ax.set_title(f"{name} patched", fontsize=12); ax.set_xlabel("position in window")
axL.set_ylabel("window index (aligned days)")
fig.suptitle("Two series, same days, patched into aligned blocks", fontsize=12, y=1.0)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

You can also stack **different variables of the same asset** into one multivariate
patch — say a stock's return *and* its volatility — so a window becomes a small
table of (days × features):

```{python}
ret: Float[Array, "n_days"] = jpm
vol: Float[Array, "n_days"] = np.abs(jpm)
w = 5
# stack two windowed series along a new feature axis:
#   (n_windows, w) ⊕ (n_windows, w)  →  (n_windows, w, n_features)
multi: Float[Array, "n_windows w n_features"] = np.stack(
    [windows(ret, w), windows(vol, w)], axis=-1
)
print(f"multivariate patch tensor: {multi.shape}   (windows, days_in_window, features)")
print("one window — columns are [return, |return|]:")
print(np.round(multi[100], 4))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## The Pattern
Patching is just *reshaping*: a 1-D series → a 2-D matrix (windows × positions); a
set of series → a 3-D tensor (windows × positions × variables).  Everything
downstream is a measurement on those rows.
:::

## 6 · What You Can Measure With Patches

Patches turn vague questions into computable ones.  A few, in increasing richness —
all of them just statistics on the patch matrix:

- **Per-window summaries** — the mean, the standard deviation (volatility), the
  worst day.  Plot per-window volatility and the clustering from §3 becomes a line.
- **Structure *within* a window** — how the positions relate.  For raw returns the
  positions are nearly independent (signs don't repeat); for *volatility* they are
  correlated (turbulence persists).  That is the seed of **total correlation**.
- **Structure *between* two windowed blocks** — how a window of X relates to the
  window of Y, the seed of **mutual information between blocks**.

The within-window contrast, shown directly:

```{python}
#| label: fig-within-structure
#| fig-cap: "Correlation between window positions (w=8) for raw returns vs |returns|. Raw returns are near-zero off the diagonal — the days in a window barely relate (signs don't repeat). |returns| shows positive off-diagonal structure — volatility persists across the window. That off-diagonal mass is the redundancy a within-block measure adds up."
def position_corr(series: Float[Array, "n_days"], w: int) -> Float[Array, "w w"]:
    """Correlation between the w window positions:  Corr = (1/n)·ZᵀZ.

    Standardize each column (a window position) to mean 0, std 1, then the
    Gram of the standardized patch matrix Z IS the correlation matrix.
    """
    Pw: Float[Array, "n_windows w"] = windows(series, w)
    Z: Float[Array, "n_windows w"] = (Pw - Pw.mean(0)) / (Pw.std(0) + 1e-9)
    n = Z.shape[0]
    # Corr = (1/n)·ZᵀZ  — contract the window axis, leaving a w×w position gram
    return einx.dot("n i, n j -> i j", Z, Z) / n

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 4.3))
for ax, data, name in [(axL, jpm, "raw returns r"), (axR, np.abs(jpm), "|returns|")]:
    C: Float[Array, "w w"] = position_corr(data, 8)
    im = ax.imshow(C, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\nmean off-diag = {C[np.triu_indices(8, 1)].mean():+.2f}",
                 fontsize=11)
    ax.set_xlabel("position"); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
axL.set_ylabel("position")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=[axL, axR], fraction=0.025, label="correlation")
plt.show()
```

The lesson of the two panels: switching from `r` to `|r|` did not clean the data —
it changed the *question* from "do returns repeat?" (no) to "does turbulence
persist?" (yes).  Same patches, different variable, opposite answer.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Where the Real Measures Live
The heatmaps above are correlation, the simplest within-block statistic.  Summing
the Gaussian information across those off-diagonals gives **total correlation**;
doing the same *between* two blocks gives **block mutual information**.  Both — and
the honest check that overlap isn't manufacturing the result — are worked through
in [Tool 3 · Windows](../dependence/labs/lab-tool3-windows.qmd) and the
[mutual information](../dependence/04-windows-and-blocks.qmd) chapter.
:::

## What the Labs Reload From Here

The **windows** and **mutual-information** labs do not re-derive any of the above:
they reload this one recipe — the `windows()` helper, a lagged block of a single
asset, and the sector-block windowing — then choose a window length and a stride and
run their measure.  The cell below is the complete, copy-pasteable handoff; it prints
the shapes and a few rows so a lab can confirm it loaded exactly what this chapter
built.

```{python}
#| label: lab-recipe
import numpy as np
from lectures import datasets
from jaxtyping import Float          # shape annotations: Float[Array, "n_days"]

Array = np.ndarray

# --- the reusable helper (identical to §1) -------------------------------------
def windows(series: Float[Array, "n_days"], w: int) -> Float[Array, "n_windows w"]:
    """Sliding w-day patches of a 1-D series → (n − w + 1, w) matrix.

    patch:  Pᵢ = (sᵢ, sᵢ₊₁, …, sᵢ₊w₋₁)   — row i is the window starting on day i.
    """
    s: Float[Array, "n_days"] = np.asarray(series, dtype=float)
    if w <= 1:
        return s.reshape(-1, 1)
    # sliding_window_view is a no-copy view of shape (n − w + 1, w)
    return np.lib.stride_tricks.sliding_window_view(s, w)

R = datasets.load_returns()           # prepared 14-stock panel (date × ticker)
meta = datasets.load_basket_meta()    # ticker → label, sector

# --- (a) lagged block of ONE asset: a causal w-day window of JPM --------------
w = 3
asset_block: Float[Array, "n_windows w"] = windows(R["JPM"].to_numpy(), w)   # row i = [r_{i}, r_{i+1}, r_{i+2}]
print(f"(a) lagged asset block  JPM, w={w}:  shape {asset_block.shape}")
print(np.round(asset_block[:3], 4))

# --- (b) sector block: patch two members of one sector on the SAME days -------
#     Banks = JPM,BAC,C,WFC,GS — take two members, window each, keep them aligned.
banks = meta.loc[meta["sector"] == "Banks", "ticker"].tolist()
a, b = banks[0], banks[1]                         # JPM, BAC
Pa: Float[Array, "n_windows w"] = windows(R[a].to_numpy(), w)   # aligned: row i is the same
Pb: Float[Array, "n_windows w"] = windows(R[b].to_numpy(), w)   #          3 calendar days for both
# stack the two aligned blocks along a new member axis:
#   (n_windows, w) ⊕ (n_windows, w)  →  (n_windows, n_members, w)
sector_block: Float[Array, "n_windows n_members w"] = np.stack([Pa, Pb], axis=1)
print(f"\n(b) sector block  {a}+{b} (Banks), w={w}:  shape {sector_block.shape}"
      "   (windows, members, positions)")
print("one aligned window — rows are members, columns are days:")
print(np.round(sector_block[100], 4))
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The Lab Contract
[Tool 3 · Windows](../dependence/labs/lab-tool3-windows.qmd) and
[Tool 3 · Mutual Information](../gaussianization/labs/lab-tool3-mutual-information.qmd)
**reload this windowing recipe and do not re-derive it.**  The `windows()` helper, the
lagged single-asset block, and the aligned sector block are defined *here*, once; a lab
imports the prepared panel, rebuilds these blocks with this exact recipe, and shows one
row before measuring.  The **only** lab-specific step those labs add is a choice of
**window length `w`** and **overlapping vs non-overlapping stride** (§4) — the modelling
knobs the measure is sensitive to.  Everything else — the data, the alignment, the block
shapes — comes from this chapter.
:::
